items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover Europe's ancient forests were nothing like we imagined
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Scientists have uncovered evidence that Europe was dominated for more than 20 million years by open woodlands, colorful meadows, and large grazing animals, not the dense forests long considered its natural state. The surprising discovery challenges modern reforestation strategies, suggesting that planting thick forests could actually harm the biodiversity conservationists hope to protect.

items.title: [New Atlas] Solar plane soars to 47,600 ft, on target to fly 100 hours
items.content_html:
A solar-powered aircraft with a 59-ft (18-m) wingspan has spent 29 hours flying over the island of Fuerteventura, running, even at night, on nothing but stored sunlight. UAVOS says its ApusNeo is the first solar plane to fly at 47,600 ft (14,500 m) in European airspace, and the company wants to put it to work watching for wildfires, one of the archipelago's biggest summer headaches.

items.title: [science.org] AI identifies individual ovenbirds from songs with 96% accuracy
items.content_html: Researchers used an artificial intelligence model to identify individual male ovenbirds from their songs with up to 96% accuracy in a test of Alberta recordings. The approach could help track which birds return to breeding territories without capturing and banding them, although it does not provide all the health information that handling birds can reveal. In a separate account, animal-behavior professor Phil Starks describes hearing clicks near an acorn barnacle on Washington’s Olympic Peninsula. He says the observation did not prove the barnacle made the sound; synchronized video and audio could test the link.

items.title: [sciencedaily.com] Researchers identify heme in 115-million-year-old Brazilian dinosaur fossil
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

An international research team says it has found mineralized structures resembling red blood cells and heme, a molecule associated with hemoglobin, in a 115-million-year-old Aratasaurus museunacionali fossil from northeastern Brazil. The team describes the findings, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, as the first chemical confirmation of heme-derived molecules inside structures interpreted as dinosaur blood cells. The team says the structures lay inside the bone’s vascular canals and that the surrounding sediment lacked the same heme signature. It proposes that the mineral hausmannite helped preserve the structures and associated molecules; rapid burial in a low-oxygen setting may also have slowed decay. Paleontologist Mary Schweitzer, who was not involved in the study, disputes whether the evidence definitively identifies heme within the cell-like structures, noting that the chemical analysis covered the whole bone. The researchers say fossilization may have distorted the structures’ shape and that further work is needed to interpret it.

items.title: [sciencealert.com] Octopus study maps two tactics for squeezing through tight openings
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers have documented how common octopuses change their movements to pass through small openings, adding a step when a gap is narrower than the distance between their eyes. For the study, published in the Journal of Experimental Biology, researchers filmed octopuses probing openings with an arm, passing other arms through, then using them to pull the rest of the body through. In tighter gaps, the animals passed their remaining arms through before squeezing the mantle and head through separately. The experiments included three subadult common octopuses. A report on the study also described tests involving four Mayan octopuses, which did not attempt to pass through the narrower openings. The researchers say the movement patterns could inform the design of soft robots for search and rescue, where current slender designs leave limited room for equipment. An octopus-like robot would need flexible arms that can both squeeze through gaps and pull the rest of the machine forward.

items.title: [3dprinting.com] 3D-printed tungsten tiles withstand 74 plasma discharges in fusion test
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Full-size 3D-printed tungsten tiles survived 74 plasma discharges inside the DIII-D National Fusion Facility in San Diego, remaining intact after about four minutes of total plasma exposure over three days. The test subjected industrial-scale printed components to conditions relevant to fusion-reactor hardware, including intense heat and particle bombardment. Researchers from North Carolina State University, Oak Ridge National Laboratory and Japanese manufacturer JEOL made the tiles using electron-beam powder bed fusion, keeping the tungsten powder bed above 1,400°C during printing to limit cracking. The parts still await detailed erosion and surface analysis after a radiation survey.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Dead stars could break one of physics' most famous limits
items.content_html: A surprising new discovery suggests that some dead stars can grow far more massive than scientists once thought possible. Computer simulations show that powerful magnetic fields could allow white dwarfs to reach 2.4 times the mass of the Sun, dramatically exceeding a famous limit that has stood for decades. The findings could help explain unusually bright supernova explosions that have long puzzled astronomers.

items.title: [phys.org] Octopuses use different escape moves to squeeze through tight holes
items.content_html: Experiments show that young common octopuses use different escape movements depending on whether an opening is wider or narrower than the distance between their eyes, a measure of the stiff cartilage around the brain. For wider holes, the animals thread several arms through, then brace against the wall to pull their head, mantle and remaining arms through. At narrower holes, they send all their arms through first, then compress the mantle and pull the rest of the body through. The team tested three common octopuses and four Mayan octopuses in clear boxes with openings sized relative to each animal’s eye-to-eye distance. Mayan octopuses avoided the narrower opening, and the researchers cautioned that the small sample and unsuccessful attempts limit how broadly the results apply. The researchers say the movement strategies could inform soft-bodied search-and-rescue robots, which currently tend to use slender, snake-like designs.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover that a clogged filter could revolutionize oil refining
items.content_html: Scientists have developed a remarkable new membrane that separates crude oil at room temperature, using the oil itself to create microscopic filtration channels. items.title: [ScienceDaily] A clever molecular trick unlocks previously impossible properties in glass
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered how to reprogram the internal structure of glass using a special molecule that rearranges chemical bonds while lowering the melting temperature. The breakthrough could unlock entirely new glass materials with precisely controlled magnetic and optical properties, opening possibilities for advanced electronics, sensors, and other technologies.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover mysterious “lonely” brain waves linked to memory loss
items.content_html: Scientists have uncovered a surprising link between Alzheimer’s-related protein buildup, disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, and fading memory. The findings suggest that hidden changes in how the brain processes memories overnight may contribute to age-related memory loss long before Alzheimer’s symptoms appear.

items.title: [science.org] Siberian tomb yields earliest direct evidence of cannabis intoxication
items.content_html: Researchers have identified what they describe as the earliest direct archaeological evidence of cannabis use for its psychoactive effects in a 2,800-year-old burial mound in southern Siberia. The study, published in Science, combines evidence from more than 1,400 cannabis seeds and chemical traces in human hair from the Tunnug 1 tomb. The findings predate previously known archaeological indications of cannabis use in China by about 300 years. Radiocarbon dating placed the seeds in the early eighth century B.C. Researchers detected cannabinol, a breakdown product of THC, and weaker signals consistent with THC in preserved hair. Together, the findings support exposure to psychoactive cannabis, although the seeds alone could not establish how the plant was used. The burial included extensive horse sacrifices and scattered human bones. The researchers suggest cannabis may have featured in funerary rites, but the idea that it was used to calm people facing sacrifice remains speculative. Independent experts questioned whether hair testing can distinguish consumption from contact with smoke or plant material; another archaeologist defended the approach. The team has begun sequencing seed DNA to investigate the plant’s history and spread.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] NASA is racing against time to save the Hubble Space Telescope
items.content_html: NASA is exploring a daring plan to save the legendary Hubble Space Telescope from its eventual fiery plunge into Earth's atmosphere. After more than 35 years of groundbreaking discoveries, Hubble is slowly losing altitude, and without intervention, it could fall back to Earth as early as 2033 or 2034. To keep the iconic observatory operating, NASA is asking private space companies to propose innovative ways to boost Hubble into a higher orbit, upgrade its capabilities, or safely dispose of it when its mission finally ends.

items.title: [science.org] JWST image-processing method boosts exoplanet sensitivity up to 15-fold
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Astronomers have developed a physics-based method to remove residual starlight from James Webb Space Telescope images, improving sensitivity to faint planets by two to 15 times and revealing the known giant exoplanet 51 Eridani b at a wavelength where earlier processing failed. The method, called Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets, or FLIP, models the telescope’s optics and adjusts for small changes that make conventional reference-star images imperfect matches. The method works with existing observations without changes to telescope hardware. The team is now reprocessing the hundreds of coronagraphic images JWST has collected to look for additional planets. Researchers say the approach could ease strict stability requirements for future observatories, but further work is needed to reduce computing costs and test it on larger data sets.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] SLAC scientists find conclusive proof of a mysterious third type of magnetism
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

For nearly 90 years, scientists believed magnetism fell into just two categories, but researchers have now confirmed a remarkable third type called altermagnetism. Using specialized X-rays, they uncovered a unique magnetic signature that proves these materials behave differently from conventional magnets. Altermagnets combine stability with the ability to efficiently carry information, potentially overcoming major limitations in today's electronics. The discovery could lead to faster computers, more efficient data centers, and breakthroughs in quantum technology.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists trick cancer cells into making the drugs that kill them
items.content_html: Scientists have developed a promising new cancer-fighting strategy that uses carbon monoxide naturally produced by tumor cells to manufacture powerful drugs inside the cancer cells themselves. Early laboratory experiments suggest the technique could selectively attack cancer while sparing healthy cells, potentially paving the way for safer chemotherapy alternatives.

items.title: [discovermagazine.com] NASA engineers extend Voyager 1 operations before one-light-day mark
items.content_html: NASA engineers have kept Voyager 1’s remaining science instruments running longer by replacing three power-hungry heating devices with lower-power alternatives, as the probe approaches a distance of one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026. Engineers completed the change, called the “Big Bang,” in September to delay another instrument shutdown that otherwise could have come by summer 2027. The probe, launched in 1977, briefly stopped communicating after scheduled communication attempts on Oct. 18 and 19; its signal returned on Oct. 20. Engineers found that a set of thrusters had gone offline and the spacecraft had automatically switched to its backup, but NASA’s Voyager team has not identified the cause of the interruption. On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be about 16.09 billion miles from Earth, with a 24-hour one-way signal delay and a 48-hour round trip.

items.title: [sci.news] CERN experiment reports first evidence of ultra-rare beauty meson decay
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The LHCb collaboration at CERN reported the first evidence of a neutral beauty meson (B⁰) decaying into two muons, a process predicted to occur about once in every 10 billion such particles. Combining the new result with earlier LHCb data gave the signal a statistical significance of 3.2 standard deviations—enough to count as evidence, but below the five-standard-deviation threshold for a discovery. The measured rate is consistent with the Standard Model, the leading theory of particle physics. Rare decays can be sensitive to effects from particles that are not produced directly in collisions. Researchers plan to continue collecting data into the early 2030s to refine the measurement; a further detector upgrade is also planned.

items.title: [Nautilus] Could One Brain Region Be Tied to Feeling Sick All Over?
items.content_html:
When you break your foot, the pain is mostly confined to your foot. When you get the flu or another systemic infection, your entire being aches: Lethargy creeps into your limbs, your appetite vanishes, your temperature jags between scorching and chilled to the bone, and you just want to pull the covers over your head.

This kind of overpowering mind-body malaise is known as “sickness syndrome,” and it’s considered a distinct physiological and emotional state. Scientists believe sickness syndrome helps the body prepare to fight infections, but they don’t fully understand what is happening in the brain when this storm cloud descends.

Read more: “How to Unlearn a Disease”

items.title: [ScienceDaily] The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
items.content_html: A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism could help explain why people with anxiety or PTSD sometimes experience intense fear in completely safe situations.

One day, he netted a few, put them in a jar, and brought them home to observe. The next morning, they were all dead. Val was devastated but intrigued.

The usual caveats apply regarding whether or not such an aging clock is actually measuring biological age, or would still produce decent data if an anti-aging intervention were involved, but gathering more data on the performance of such clocks is nonetheless a potentially useful activity. items.title: [ScienceDaily] All 5 genetic “letters” of DNA and RNA discovered in a 4.5-billion-year-old asteroid
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered all five essential nucleobases used in DNA and RNA in pristine samples from asteroid Ryugu, revealing that key ingredients for life existed in space billions of years ago. The remarkable finding adds to growing evidence from other asteroids and meteorites that these molecules were widespread throughout the early Solar System.
